faq.a: The amygdala is a small, almond-shaped part deep inside your brain. It works like a smoke alarm, spotting danger and setting off big feelings like fear and anger very fast.
asks: What part of the brain controls fear?

faq.q: Why can I not think clearly when I am upset?
faq.a: When the alarm rings, your brain puts its energy into staying safe, so the thinking and planning part goes quiet for a while. Once you calm down, it switches back on.
asks: Why do I forget things when I am upset?

faq.q: How do I switch off my brain's alarm?
faq.a: Breathe slowly, in through your nose and out through your mouth, a few times. Slow breathing tells your body you are safe, so the alarm settles and you can think again.
asks: How do I calm my brain down?

faq.q: Is my brain's alarm a bad thing?
faq.a: No, it keeps you safe, like pulling your hand from a hot pan. Sometimes it rings for things that are not really dangerous, like a test, and then you can help it calm down.

faq.q: Do grown-ups get big feelings too?
faq.a: Yes, everyone does. Grown-ups have had more practice calming down, and the thinking part of their brain has finished growing, so it can often step in a little faster.

facts: People have two amygdalae, one on each side of the brain, each about the size of an almond.
The prefrontal cortex, the brain's planning area behind your forehead, is one of the last parts to finish developing, usually in the mid-twenties.
